claims.quote: atop, abed, ahorse

claims.claim: Martin builds well over a hundred two-root compounds from short native words and coins his world-vocabulary by the same compounding.
claims.quote: weirwood, greensight, skinchanger, ironborn, sellsword

claims.claim: The medieval-fantasy feel comes from the frequency of compounds rather than from any single coinage.
The style veers between functional modern thriller prose and prose padded with fake medievalisms, sometimes on the same page.
claims.quote: veers from purely functional modern thriller prose

claims.claim: Martin's baseline register is plain and functional, with periodic flashes of limpid beauty, notably in Arya's chapters.
claims.quote: The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional

claims.claim: He repeats a small set of words within a passage (cool, still) to build stillness and mood.
claims.quote: repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still'

claims.claim: Confrontations are carried by short, charged exchanges that deliver the revelations rather than by narration.
claims.quote: terse, charged dialogue

claims.claim: He makes familiar words strange by slight deformation and adds wholly coined medieval-sounding words (sellsword, smallfolk).
claims.quote: slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases

claims.claim: The would-be medievalisms harden into mannerisms that annoy on repetition.
claims.quote: would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms

claims.claim: Martin reuses fixed descriptors like a Homeric epithet system, with 'black as night' appearing four times nearly unchanged.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
claims.quote: Stock phrases are thermals

claims.claim: No single sentence is especially strong; the prose works by volley, which the author calls shotgun writing.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
claims.quote: No single sentence is that effective

claims.claim: Stock phrases work by triggering recognition rather than fresh visualisation, which keeps the reading fast.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
claims.quote: We are cognitively lazy with the familiar.

claims.claim: Character speech is consistently more memorable than the surrounding narrative description.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
claims.quote: Dialogue would shine brightest

claims.claim: Bodies and moods are rendered through a recurring kit of phrases (faces still as masks, men corded with muscle).
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
claims.quote: Faces still as masks, faces dark with anger

claims.claim: Martin hovers close at the character's shoulder but steps back to narratorial distance at odd moments, mixing the character's word for a person with the narrator's full name in one paragraph.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Unseen Plane Crash: Psychic Distance'
claims.quote: take[s] a big step backwards at odd times

claims.claim: An evaluative adverb in narration ('Stupidly, Jon argued') fuses narrator judgment with the character's own.
claims.quote: Stupidly, Jon argued

claims.claim: Italicised thought grew by roughly six percent across the series and is weakest when it states the obvious or jogs memory.
Calling one person 'her father', 'Ned Stark', 'Father', and 'Eddard Stark' within a scene signals unsteady narrative distance.
A word like 'Even' in narration marks the POV character's perspective without an explicit thought tag.
A handful of relics (must needs, soon or late, near as) supply historical flavour in place of consistent period language.
claims.quote: a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer

claims.claim: Words such as pug-nosed, longshoreman (1811), condone (1857), yen, burp, and snark leak modern English into Westeros.
claims.quote: shows you the seams of his work

claims.claim: Many sentences are modular and deletable: a 1,897-word passage compresses to 427 words using only topic sentences.
claims.quote: modular sentences that can snap together like LEGO

claims.claim: Frequent single-sentence paragraphs sustain narrative momentum.
claims.quote: Martin has a fair number of one-lines

claims.claim: Some similes misfire on tempo (brigands melting like snow) or on verb-modifier logic (glowering through a beard), and redundant paired adjectives recur.
claims.quote: low, quiet voice

claims.claim: Sentences devoted to coldness pile up and could be cut by about half.
Around 250 zeugmatic sentences occur in roughly 148,130 sentences, most often about the body and about sky or weather.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Zeugma and Literary DNA'
claims.quote: The day was warm and cloudless, the sky a deep blue.

claims.claim: Mid-speech attribution and action beats are placed to work as extra punctuation and control the reader's ear; the ideal exchange is untagged.
claims.quote: tags, when strategically placed, can serve as extra punctuation

claims.claim: In A Game of Thrones semicolons and colons are used interchangeably (three on one page), a habit corrected by A Dance with Dragons.
claims.quote: he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now

claims.feature: purple register for nature and violence
claims.claim: The tone swings from casual to purple, with ornate diction reserved for wilderness (green) and bloodshed (red).
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
claims.quote: the tone can be very casual and very purple

claims.claim: Combat passages personify the sword and stretch or stop time.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
claims.quote: time slept when swords woke

claims.claim: Backstory is delivered as monologue dressed as dialogue, assigned to talkative characters as a trait, lampshaded, or reported in summary rather than quoted.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Now, As We All Know'
claims.quote: It is a flashback dressed up as a monologue

claims.claim: Chapters cycle among coercion, negotiation, action, travel, revelation, predicament, and disclosure scenes, each shoehorning in secondary information.
claims.quote: The narrative cycles between these types of scene.

claims.claim: A chapter opens in medias res on a small crisis, slides from past perfect into simple past for a compressed memory, then returns to the present.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Short-Hop Flashback'
claims.quote: past perfect melds into the simple past tense

claims.claim: Martin permits himself narratorial distance only when temporal distance justifies it.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Short-Hop Flashback'
claims.quote: only with temporal distance will he permit himself some narrative distance

claims.claim: Catchphrases and nicknames make thin characters stick (Walder Frey's heh, Hodor, Gregor's seventeen lines).
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Making a Memorable Character'
claims.quote: Gregor Clegane: 17 lines

claims.claim: Movement sentences chain prepositional phrases to carry the reader through space.
claims.quote: They passed beneath the gatehouse, over the drawbridge

claims.claim: Narration slips into the character's own idiom for a phrase, a move the essay flags as free indirect.
claims.quote: A little free indirect!

claims.claim: Double meanings are exploited in a single word (rams that lap at water).
claims.quote: cruel iron rams lapping at the water

claims.claim: Characters are built by others' talk long before they speak; Stannis is named 98 times before appearing.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Your Reputation Precedes You'
claims.quote: Stannis is mentioned 98 times before he appears

claims.claim: Bodily detail is used as psychological shorthand, and dialogue exposes social hierarchy.
claims.quote: Martin's dialogue does a great job of revealing social dynamics.

claims.claim: Moral greyness is rendered as interior monologue that holds two impulses in one paragraph.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Inside the House of Black and White'
claims.quote: part of him wanted to call out

claims.claim: Martin defends tight third because people perceive only from their own eyes.
claims.quote: see the events around us from our own eyes

claims.claim: He drafts several consecutive chapters in one character's voice and needs days to recover a voice after switching.
claims.quote: I get into a character's voice

claims.feature: emotional cost as craft test (Martin's words)
claims.claim: Martin treats a scene's difficulty to write as the measure of its effect on the reader.
claims.quote: If it's hard to write, it'll be hard to read, too.

claims.claim: Recurring sayings are deliberate and modelled on Stephen King, despite reader annoyance.
claims.quote: I do it intentionally

claims.claim: Each POV character carries a distinct voice and vocabulary, which makes switching exhausting.
claims.quote: its own voice and vocabulary

claims.claim: Martin rejects the omniscient viewpoint outright as false to human perception.
claims.quote: I actually hate the omniscient viewpoint.

claims.claim: Martin describes fantasy's proper language as dreamlike and defined by taste, colour, and texture.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, 'On Fantasy' (1996), georgerrmartin.com
claims.quote: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.

claims.claim: He frames the reader's motive as recovering vividness of colour, which underwrites his heraldic and food description.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, 'On Fantasy' (1996), georgerrmartin.com
claims.quote: We read fantasy to find the colors again

claims.claim: Martin conveyed Dothraki in the novels by altering English syntax and sentence rhythm rather than inventing a language.
claims.quote: playing with the syntax and sentence rhythms a bit

claims.claim: Martin says he wants books richly textured and full of sensory detail so the reader experiences rather than reads.
claims.quote: richly textured and full of sensory detail

claims.feature: interior access prose can do (Martin's words)
claims.claim: Martin cites a lying-tag sentence as the kind of interiority prose gives that film cannot.
claims.quote: 'Yes you can trust me,' he lied

claims.claim: Martin's TV years taught him to cut scripts word by word, a habit he carries into prose.
claims.quote: trimming and tightening line by line and word by word

claims.claim: Martin ends each chapter on a tense or revelatory beat, a TV-script habit.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'A Song of Ice and Fire'
claims.quote: a twist or a cliffhanger

claims.claim: Martin treats viewpoint characters as unreliable narrators so readers must weigh the narration.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'A Song of Ice and Fire'

claims.claim: The Bran direwolf chapter came to Martin vividly and was drafted in about three days nearly as published.
claims.source: Longreads excerpt of Rolling Stone (Mikal Gilmore), 2014-04-24
claims.quote: came right out of me, almost in the form

claims.claim: From A Feast for Crows some chapters carry descriptive titles instead of the POV name.
claims.source: W.A. Hughes, 'How to Write a Chapter of ASOIAF', 2014-05-12 (satire)
claims.quote: 'The Iron Captain,' 'The Princess in the Tower'

claims.claim: Chapters typically open with the character already eating, fighting, or mid-conversation.
claims.source: W.A. Hughes, 'How to Write a Chapter of ASOIAF', 2014-05-12 (satire)

claims.claim: Characters fixate on stock expressions in italics, which the satirist reads as padding.
claims.source: W.A. Hughes, 'How to Write a Chapter of ASOIAF', 2014-05-12 (satire)
claims.quote: isn't worth a mummer's fart

claims.claim: Bran I opens on weather against conventional advice, then pivots to a long multi-clause sentence about a beheading.
claims.source: Jon Auerbach, 'Writing advice from the first chapter', 2017
claims.quote: The morning had dawned clear and cold

claims.claim: Setting facts are folded into ordinary exposition rather than explained.
claims.source: Jon Auerbach, 'Writing advice from the first chapter', 2017
claims.quote: the ninth year of summer, and the seventh of Bran's life

claims.claim: Objects are described with specific compound epithets that later gain plot weight.
claims.source: Jon Auerbach, 'Writing advice from the first chapter', 2017
claims.quote: Valyrian steel, spell-forged and dark as smoke

claims.claim: Emotion is rendered as bodily sensation through concrete simile.
claims.quote: Fear filled his gut like a meal he could not digest

claims.claim: Sword-clash is described by an unexpected animal comparison instead of the stock metallic one.
claims.quote: like an animal screaming in pain

claims.claim: Characters are introduced by paired antitheses against a sibling.
claims.quote: slender where Robb was muscular, dark where Robb was fair

claims.claim: Important moments are slowed and packed with concrete specifics rather than rushed.
Backstory enters when a remark prompts the POV character's memory rather than by narrator summary.
claims.source: Dark Jackel's Howl, 'Let's Read AGOT Part 1', 2015-08-19
claims.quote: some character makes a comment or observation, which prompts memories

claims.claim: The prologue builds dread through negative sensory statements and dialogue with double meanings.
claims.source: The Fantasy Review, 'Prologue Summary and Analysis', 2023-10-14
claims.quote: The Others made no sound

claims.claim: Battle description opens ornate and tips into graphic gore, with spatial confusion left intentional.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), Tyrion VIII, 2014-01-30
claims.quote: iron rose, thorns gleaming

claims.claim: Earlier physical detail (Bran's gargoyle handholds) is re-used as an instrument of later violence.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), Bran VII ACOK, 2016-04-07
claims.quote: His tongue felt strange and thick in his mouth

claims.claim: A repeated phrase in a doomed POV ('the bloody snow') carries foreshadowing the character cannot read.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), ASOS Prologue, 2016-04-18

claims.claim: Fan close readers note full names in narration assert agency while 'the dwarf' appears ten times in one depressed Tyrion chapter.
Jaime's italic commentary goes silent immediately before a violent act, forcing the reader to register it.
claims.quote: absolutely SILENT

claims.claim: 'Nuncle' and similar archaisms (pease, neeps) appear only from A Feast for Crows onward, a deliberate late shift some readers dislike.
claims.quote: It's totally an AFFC and onward thing

claims.claim: A phrase like 'Only the cold' recurs across Jon's death-adjacent moments to bind them.
claims.quote: Only the cold

claims.claim: Reading-group posters contrast Martin's crisp, fast, gritty prose with Kay's slow lyricism, while one flags excessive wordiness.
claims.source: Goodreads Sword & Laser thread, 'Kay or Martin?'
claims.quote: fast where Kay is slow; gritty where Kay is lyrical

claims.claim: Each chapter is named for its POV and the reader knows only what that character knows, who may be an unreliable witness.
claims.quote: the reader only knows what the main character knows

claims.claim: An editor's first-50 review credits titled POV chapters with removing head-hopping confusion and praises exposition delivered in scene.
claims.quote: giving each character a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably

claims.claim: Description flows without Tolkien-style descriptive excess and each character keeps a distinct voice.
claims.quote: fluid lyricism, without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium

claims.claim: Sanderson's lecture uses 'Bran Stark' in chapter one as a tone promise of bleakness.
claims.quote: is a tone promise

claims.claim: Ser, southron, and craven date to 1451, 1488, and 1400; turncloak is an archaic-sounding remake of turncoat; 'butt' and 'ass' jar.
claims.quote: Martin's archaic-sounding amendment of turncoat

claims.claim: Different cultures are marked by colloquial phrases and aphorisms such as 'words are wind'.
Martin uses accurate late-Middle-English words sparingly, avoids thou/thee, and keeps modern syntax.
claims.quote: sweet spot between Modern and Middle English

claims.feature: lexical cohesion and register by class
claims.claim: Repeated insult words bind paragraphs, 'without' means outside, and m'Lord versus my Lord marks class; lexical density about 4–4.5 and a sixth-grade readability index.
claims.quote: Terms like 'elsewise'

claims.claim: Text-mining across four series finds Martin uses -ly adverbs least and reads at about age ten by readability index.
claims.source: Winter Is Coming (Dan Selcke) on Dimitris Spathis, 2015-09-24
claims.quote: George R.R. Martin hates adverbs

claims.claim: AGOT scores Flesch Reading Ease 87, has 851 sentences over 30 words, 3.39% slow-paced paragraphs, and near-equal standard versus alternative dialogue tags with adverbs in tags flagged.
claims.source: AutoCrit, 'What's the Score? A Game of Thrones'
claims.quote: Flesch Reading Ease score of 87

claims.claim: 'Mummer's farce' recurs constantly and 'jape' reads as a pretentious substitute for joke; prose 'borders on serviceable'.
claims.quote: at least ten times in every book

claims.claim: Hodor's and Reek's repeated lines become formula rather than characterisation.
Sex scenes fixate on nipple size and colour and crude similes, unlike his assured violence and heraldry.
claims.quote: not good at writing about sex

claims.claim: Feasts are rendered as course-by-course lists with taste and smell, and appetite indexes a character's mental state.
claims.quote: flavored with fear

claims.claim: Meal descriptions mark inclusion, class, and culture, with sensory verbs carrying the emotion.
Martin describes loving a Tyrion chapter, then rereading it and deciding it failed.
claims.quote: I wrote a Tyrion chapter I just loved

claims.claim: Martin says he has always written in tight third person because that is how people perceive: we see events from our own eyes and hear only our own thoughts.
claims.quote: I've always written from a tight third-person point of view

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a strong believer in a limited but very tight third person and says he hates the omniscient viewpoint because no one has one.
claims.quote: limited but very tight third person point of view

claims.claim: Each POV chapter is written in a different voice and style; Martin says he switches voice every time he switches chapters.
claims.source: Entertainment Weekly (James Hibberd, 2018-11-19) via Winter Is Coming
claims.quote: I switch voices every time I switch chapters.

claims.claim: Moving from Tyrion chapters to Jon Snow chapters is a whole different voice, and Martin struggles for days to recover a character's voice after switching.
claims.quote: it's a whole different voice

claims.claim: Martin does not write chapters in reading order; because shifting voices is hard he drafts two to four consecutive chapters of the same character.
claims.quote: write consecutively two, three or four chapters

claims.claim: Martin says multiple viewpoints are essential so the reader sees a conflict from both sides' self-justifications rather than a cartoon Dark Lord.
claims.quote: Having multiple viewpoints is crucial to the grayness of the characters.

claims.claim: Apparent contradictions between chapters are deliberate: two characters remember an event differently because of the point-of-view structure and the unreliable narrator.
claims.quote: the point of view structure and the unreliable narrator

claims.claim: Martin describes his method as seeing everything only through the eyes of the viewpoint characters, a discipline he links to structure learned in television.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: seeing everything through the eyes only of the viewpoint characters

claims.feature: first viewpoint character as decoy hero
claims.claim: Martin opens with Bran as the first viewpoint so readers assume he is the young-Arthur hero, then defenestrates him to signal this is not the familiar story.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: Bran is the first viewpoint character.

claims.claim: For battles Martin alternates between dropping the reader into the carnage from a private's viewpoint and looking down from a general's vantage.
claims.source: Interview with George R. R. Martin, bernardcornwell.net (undated)
claims.quote: Sometimes I employ the private's viewpoint

claims.claim: Martin traces the interwoven multi-POV structure of the novels to the Wild Cards mosaic novels, likening it to a Robert Altman film in prose.
claims.quote: Robert Altman film in prose

claims.claim: Martin modeled the general construction on The Lord of the Rings: begin small, accumulate characters, then send them on separate paths.
claims.quote: Tolkien begins very small, in the Shire

claims.feature: register: modern prose with a pinch of archaism
claims.claim: Martin says the line between modern prose and archaic diction is fine; his compromise is modern prose stripped of pop-culture references with occasional archaic words, like salt in soup.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: modern prose, but omitting all pop culture references

claims.claim: After his editor feared a 'forsooth' would follow, Martin kept 'mayhaps' for old characters like Aemon and gave younger ones like Bran 'perhaps' and 'maybe'.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: a "forsooth" would follow shortly

claims.feature: period register by reading period syntax
claims.claim: For Fevre Dream Martin read period novels such as Twain's to absorb their syntax and vocabulary, a different register strategy from the one used in Ice and Fire.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, UK Signing Tour Nottingham report (2005-10-20)
claims.quote: to understand the syntax and words

claims.claim: Unlike Tolkien, Martin invents only the words he needs (he says about eight Dothraki words) and admits he fakes the rest.
claims.source: IGN interview (May 2019) via Winter Is Coming (2019-05-14)
claims.quote: He invented entire languages, I just fake it.

claims.feature: names as slant-variants with phonetic power
claims.claim: Martin makes names up as variants of real ones (Eddard for Edward) and insists on the right sound, holding that a name evokes a character better than a page of description.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Naming Characters correspondence (2003-04-01)
claims.quote: variants of real names -- Eddard for Edward

claims.feature: names: Vance and Tolkien as models
claims.claim: Asked about names, Martin points the fan to Jack Vance and Tolkien as the masters of evocative naming.
claims.source: So Spake Martin, Naming Characters correspondence (2003-04-01)
claims.quote: He's marvelous with names.

claims.claim: Martin denies that Ice and Fire is Vancean; he tried once to write like Vance and concluded only Vance can, keeping his own plainer voice.
claims.quote: Vance has his voice and I have mine.

claims.feature: Vance admired for ear for language
claims.claim: What Martin says sets Vance apart is style, imagination, world building and an ear for names and language.
claims.quote: His ear for names, for language.

claims.claim: Martin says his early style piled on adjectives, mistaking verbosity for richness, until journalism-school professors struck them out.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: if one adjective was good, three were better

claims.claim: Hearing actors read his long speeches taught Martin to write shorter back-and-forth dialogue instead of page-long monologues.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: much shorter back and forth kind of dialogue

claims.claim: Martin credits his television years with sharpening his dialogue.
claims.source: January Magazine profile, Linda L. Richards (Jan 2001)
claims.quote: I think working in Hollywood sharpened my dialog.

claims.claim: Martin says screenwriting is easier than prose because, per William Goldman, it is all structure and dialogue, and that working in TV improved both in his novels.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: It's all structure, structure and dialogue.

claims.claim: Martin carries television act breaks into chapter endings: each should close on a cliffhanger, a twist point, or a new revelation.
claims.source: TIFF Master Class (June 2012), transcript excerpts at Bulletproof Screenwriting
claims.quote: just a twist point or a new revelation

claims.claim: Though no volume resolves the whole, Martin tries to give each book a sense of completion like a symphony movement wrapping up.
claims.quote: a movement of the symphony has wrapped up

claims.claim: Martin calls himself a very visual writer who sees a scene in his head the way a director sees a shot.
claims.source: January Magazine profile, Linda L. Richards (Jan 2001)
claims.quote: much as a director would see a shot

claims.feature: chapter opening from a seed sentence
claims.claim: The first chapter came to Martin whole; its first sentence's phrase 'summer snows' told him seasons were wrong here, and the world grew outward from that sentence.
claims.quote: They find the direwolf pups in the summer snows.

claims.claim: Martin does not build the world first; the map took half an hour and the world-building grew parallel to the writing.
claims.source: Rolling Stone, Mikal Gilmore, The Complete Rolling Stone Interview (2014-04-23)
claims.quote: I don't build the world first, then write in it.

claims.claim: Martin defends feasts, clothes and heraldry as necessary because a novel is an immersive experience; detail and showing-not-telling are required and nothing is gratuitous.
claims.quote: detail is necessary, showing not telling is necessary

claims.claim: Martin says if his sex is gratuitous then so are his violence, feasting, clothes and heraldry, since little of it advances plot and plot is not why one reads novels.
claims.quote: gratuitous feasting, and gratuitous description of clothes

claims.claim: In the cookbook foreword Martin says he wants readers to live with the story rather than read it, and to taste the food when they sit at his table.
claims.source: Official Game of Thrones Cookbook foreword via ComicBook.com (Nicole Drum, 2024-05-04)
claims.quote: I want them to taste the food.

claims.claim: Martin frames fiction as emotion and vicarious experience, which is why sensory detail matters more than what characters are saying.
claims.source: Official Game of Thrones Cookbook foreword via ComicBook.com (Nicole Drum, 2024-05-04)
claims.quote: Fiction is about emotion. The heart, not the head.

claims.claim: Martin admits he enjoys heraldry for its own sake and plays fast and loose with real heraldic conventions.
claims.quote: I enjoy the heraldry just for its own sake

claims.claim: Explaining his medievalism, Martin lists the sword's romance and the Middle Ages' contrasts, then adds simply that he likes the heraldry.
claims.quote: Besides, I like the heraldry.

claims.claim: Martin rejects both a Disney Middle Ages and thousands of pages of mud and lice; the real period had room for plagues and pageantry and he wants both, heightened.
claims.quote: room for both plagues and pageantry

claims.claim: Martin describes the Middle Ages as chivalry beside brutality, castles over hovels, and tournament color rising out of a world of dung, dirt and plague.
claims.quote: a brown and grey world of dung, dirt, and plague

claims.feature: black-clad good guys to undermine convention
claims.claim: Martin dressed the Night's Watch in black partly to undermine the convention that evil minions wear black.
claims.quote: to undermine that annoying convention

claims.feature: historical-fiction grit fused with fantasy wonder
claims.claim: Martin says he wanted to combine the wonder and imagery of Tolkien fantasy with the gloom of historical fiction.
claims.source: Tolkien Society report of Edinburgh International Book Festival talk (2014-08-12)
claims.quote: the wonder and image of Tolkien fantasy

claims.claim: Martin faults Tolkien's imitators for taking medieval castles and princesses but writing them from a 20th-century point of view.
claims.source: Tolkien Society report of Edinburgh International Book Festival talk (2014-08-12)
claims.quote: writing it from a 20th-century point of view

claims.claim: On his own blog Martin restates the series' aim as blending epic fantasy's wonder with the grittiness of the best historical fiction, with much less magic than most fantasy.
claims.source: Not a Blog, 'Here There Be Dragons' (2024-07-11)
claims.quote: blend the wonder of epic fantasy with the grittiness

claims.claim: Martin describes historical fiction as grittier, harder-edged and more realistic than epic fantasy and says he set out to meld the two traditions.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: grittier, harder-edged, more realistic

claims.claim: Because history locks a writer in, Martin mixes sources and amplifies them, holding that fantasy must be bigger and brighter than life (Hadrian's Wall becomes seven hundred feet of ice).

claims.quote: fantasy always has to be a little bigger and brighter

claims.claim: Martin tells writers to think through every departure from real life (flying pigs change the pork industry) and to get armor, armies and horses right or readers will write.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: it's gonna change the pork industry

claims.claim: Martin contrasts Dunsany's once-upon-a-time mode with Tolkien's dynastic history and places his own work with Tolkien, closer to historical fiction.
claims.source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
claims.quote: who was the king before him?

claims.claim: Martin says fantasy must be rooted in reality first, then played with and given its imaginative element.
claims.source: Bullseye / Sound of Young America, John Hodgman (2011-09-19)
claims.quote: In fantasy, you have to root it in reality.

claims.feature: fantasy prose as the language of dreams
claims.claim: Martin's credo essay holds that the best fantasy is written in the language of dreams and restores strong colors and spices that realism drains away.
claims.quote: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.

claims.claim: The essay opposes fantasy's rich colors and spices to the drab strip-mall real, implying a prose that reaches for vivid sensory nouns.
claims.quote: silver and scarlet, indigo and azure

claims.claim: Martin intentionally repeats phrases such as 'A Lannister always pays his debts' and remembered lines, a technique he says he took from Stephen King.
claims.quote: I have learned this technique from Stephen King

claims.claim: Martin handles magic like salt in a stew, a little improving it and too much ruining it; elsewhere he says explicit magic ceases to be magical.
claims.quote: like a little salt in a stew

claims.feature: thematic core: the heart in conflict
claims.claim: Martin quotes Faulkner that the only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself, which drives his interior POV.
claims.quote: the human heart in conflict with itself

claims.claim: Martin cites the Iliad as a model where the hero of one side is the villain of the other, shaping his multi-sided viewpoint scheme.

0.trueWording: high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin
0.note: Exact phrase in the abstract: 'his style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin'. The claim's second half is also stated verbatim in the preceding sentence: 'a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French or other languages... or the neo-classical coinages'.

1.trueWording: Almost none of these are found in Martin's work
1.note: Exact sentence follows the list of Latin/Greek prefixes ('Their absence speaks volumes'). Page then states Martin 'uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes', gives un-/be- examples, and names 'the archaic prefix a- to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse'. Every element of the claim is on the page.

2.trueWording: convey a deep sense of their Anglo-Saxon provenance
2.note: Exact phrase: 'Martin overwhelmingly uses forms which convey a deep sense of their Anglo-Saxon provenance.' All five suffixes named in the claim (-craft, -dom, -ness, -hood, -less) appear in the page's list, each glossed with an Old English etymology; the page adds these 'convey a richness and historical depth'.

3.trueWording: coin scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms
3.note: Page reads 'Martin uses this facility to coin scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms' — the quote inflects 'coin' as 'coins', so not word for word. Substance fully supported: longsword and oathbreaker appear in the compound-word list; godswood, weirwood, sellsword, dragonglass, greenseer, smallfolk and skinchanger all appear in the neologism list, and the page ties them to 'the otherness of his fantasy world'.

4.trueWording: technocratic and legalistic mindset of medieval religious inquisitors
4.note: Page has the two adjectives in the reverse order from the quote, so not verbatim. Substance holds: 'intercession' is spoken by Maester Colemon, 'a learned man, and so it is in character'; 'fornication' and 'adultery' occur in the High Septon's religious court; and the page says that 'against the overwhelming backdrop of Saxon vocabulary... the rare use of technocratic neoclassical combining words is very conspicuous'.

5.note: Exact phrase in the opening: the style 'veers from purely functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms'. The within-a-page mixing is also explicit: 'On the same page there can be ofts and elsewises from the 15th century and then things being divvied up or people asking What's that all about? as if in modern New York.'

6.note: Exact phrase: 'The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional.' The cumulative-antiquity half is supported by the conclusion: antiquity comes 'not because of the occasional pseudo-medievalisms' but because 'he consistently chooses words of Anglo-Saxon origin... giving his prose a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness'.

7.trueWording: consistently chooses words of Anglo-Saxon origin
7.note: Exact phrase in the conclusion, and the sentence continues 'and generally avoids Latinate and neoclassical vocabulary', matching the claim's second half word for word as well.

8.note: Exact phrase: 'GRRM's limpid style can have a powerfully simple beauty.' The next sentence names the POV: 'I particularly associate this with the character of Arya Stark once she's set sail from Westeros for the island city of Braavos.' Both 'limpid' and the Arya attribution are the page's own words.

9.trueWording: haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere

(-hood renders as "– hood" with an en dash in the extracted text, which is why a naive grep for "-hood" misses it; it is present at line 69 as "– hood (from the Old English -hād)".)

80.trueWording: deployed for effect in the context of legal or religious or courtly matters
80.note: Conclusion: Latinate words "are mostly excluded or only deployed for effect in the context of legal or religious or courtly matters". The maester element is explicit: "Maester Colemon says 'intercession' ... but then, he is a maester, a learnèd man, and so it is in character", plus a final chapter "about the educated maesters of Oldtown" carrying "penetrate", "complement", "complaint". The technocratic/standing-out element is also explicit: "fornication" is "deployed to convey technocratic and legalistic mindset of medieval religious inquisitors", and "the rare use of technocratic neoclassical combining words is very conspicuous". All four register contexts named in the claim (legal, religious, courtly, maester) are on the page.

81.trueWording: veers from functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms
81.note: Opening paragraph: Martin's style "is unstable. By this I mean it veers from purely functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms". The single-page element is the next sentence: "On the same page there can be 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century and then things being 'divvied up'". The claim's "faux-medievalisms" is a synonym for the page's "fake medievalisms"; everything else matches, including the thriller framing.

82.trueWording: The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional
82.note: Section 1, headed "Crisp": "The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional." "Clear" is supported by the conclusion's reference to his "otherwise swift clear style". The "despite the fantasy setting" clause is supported by: "There are a few nods in the direction of cod-medievalism, a few stylistic gestures towards the books' fantasy setting ... But these tics don't conceal the fundamental modernity of the prose."

83.trueWording: The most persistent one is removing the -ly suffix from adverbs
83.note: Section 9 ("Cod medievalism") lists as mannerisms: "The most persistent one is removing the -ly suffix from adverbs. 'He is like to be angry'; 'He has near finished the task.'", then "'Oft' instead of the sensible 'often'" and "'Elsewise'". All three cited forms are on the page. Small structural nuance: 'like to be' is given as an instance of the -ly dropping (like/likely) rather than as a separate archaism alongside oft and elsewise, but the claim's grouping does not distort the source.

84.trueWording: 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century ... as if in modern New York
84.note: Opening paragraph, verbatim: "On the same page there can be 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century and then things being 'divvied up' or people asking 'What's that all about?' as if in modern New York." Both embedded fragments were confirmed present in the raw text: "divvied up" exactly, and "What's that all about?" differing from the claim only in capitalisation and terminal question mark. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM only because the claim record carries no designated quote field.

85.trueWording: GRRM's limpid style can have a powerfully simple beauty
85.note: Section 2 ("Poetry"): "When his characters are not swearing or chopping off each others' heads, GRRM's limpid style can have a powerfully simple beauty." The phrase "powerfully simple beauty" was confirmed verbatim in the raw text, and the "outside violence" condition is exactly the source's "not swearing or chopping off each others' heads" clause. The post attaches the observation to Arya Stark's Braavos chapters.

86.trueWording: repetitions of 'cool' and 'still' — signs of haste, or careful repetitions
86.note: Parenthetical following the Water Palace passage: "(I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still' – are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.)" Both words, the single-passage scope, and the two competing readings (atmosphere vs haste) are all present. The claim's neutral "read either as" correctly preserves the author's stated undecidedness rather than picking a side.

87.trueWording: Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue
87.note: Section 4 ("Dramatic dialogue"): "Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue. As a reader on numerous occasions you experience a real dramatic shock when you realise, along with one character, the implications of another one's words, and are horrified or shocked." Both halves of the claim — terse charged dialogue, and implications landing as shock — are explicit. ("though" is the source's own typo for "through"; quoted as it stands.)

88.trueWording: coined completely new, medieval-sounding words; coin scores of neologisms
88.note: Section 6: "Martin has coined completely new, medieval-sounding words to fit the fantasy medievalism of the story ... Sept and septon and septa ..., maester (doctor/alchemist), ... warg (human who can inhabit an animal)". Section 7: "Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms: sellsword (mercenary), smallfolk (ordinary people) ... godswood ... greenseer". All seven cited words confirmed in the raw text, and the claim's split between the two categories matches the post's own two-section division. Unrelated to the claim, but the post's coinage list is loose in one spot: it includes "pyromancer", a pre-existing Greek-derived English word.

89.trueWording: slight deformation of existing standard words into something rich and strange
89.note: Section 5 ("Distorting English"): "Martin employs the slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases into something rich and strange. A frequent example is that knights ... are called 'Ser', an obvious distortion of the traditional Sir, which starts out sounding silly but, by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term. Similarly, girls who have had their first period have 'flowered'." Both examples confirmed verbatim in the raw text, and the repetition mechanism the claim cites is the source's own ("by sheer repetition", "By repetition over the multiple scenes"). The claim's "for menstruation" is a fair gloss of "girls who have had their first period".

90.trueWording: uses the word "jape" instead of joke… "aside from its pretentiousness"
90.note: Page: "Whenever he talks about someone joking around, he uses the word 'jape' instead of joke. Jape, aside from its pretentiousness, is a singularly displeasing word." The overuse framing is also supported: "Martin leans on words that I presume he thinks sound archaic and exotic. In reality they just sound ridiculous." Minor wording drift: the essay says "archaic and exotic", not "medieval" (though "faux-medieval flourishes" appears earlier in the same post). "jape" and "pretentiousness" are verbatim; the claim sentence as a whole is a paraphrase.

91.trueWording: "the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book"
91.note: FREQUENCY IS INFLATED — fix before use. Page: "Do you really need to describe every king's council and meeting between frenemies as a 'mummer's farce'? Seriously, the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book." The essay says AT LEAST TEN times per book, not "dozens". The "nearly every council and hostile meeting" half is well supported ("every king's council and meeting between frenemies"). Note: a higher count ("at least a hundred instances", "every half dozen pages") appears only in reader comments below the post, not in Gelzer-Govatos's text, so it cannot back "dozens" under this attribution.

92.trueWording: "prose borders on the servicable… faux-medieval flourishes go a bridge too far"
92.note: Closest of the fifteen to verbatim. Page: "Most of the time his prose borders on the servicable, but there are times when his faux-medieval flourishes go a bridge too far." ("servicable" is the author's own misspelling.) "faux-medieval flourishes" is verbatim; "borders on the servicable" is slightly weaker than the claim's flat "is serviceable", and the essay says "most of the time", not "otherwise".

93.trueWording: "Annoying Speech Mannerisms"; Hodor "can only say his own name"
93.note: Page section heading "Annoying Speech Mannerisms": "Martin frequently employs particular speech patters [sic]". Hodor is "a mentally handicapped stable boy who can only say his own name, Hodor". Reek: "he repeats a rhyme to remember who he is… Reek, my name is Reek, it rhymes with [random word that rhymes with Reek]", with "slight variations" (weak, squeak) — exactly the claim's "rhyme with a swapped last word". Both examples confirmed.

94.trueWording: "the scenes themselves are clunky to the extreme"… elsewhere adequate, here "he dips"
94.note: Page: "the scenes themselves are clunky to the extreme. They usually involve someone being drunk with desire for the other person, their head swimming with the wine of lust or some such nonsense" — supports "clichéd, overwrought". The register break is explicit: "If in most other areas Martin's prose acheives a level of adequatulence, in his sex scenes he dips to what I imagine is the level of writing found in those books… with titles like The Incredible Hunk". The essay's own vocabulary is "clunky"/"dire"/"slimy", not "disconnected from the surrounding register".

95.trueWording: "the real Martinian stock phrases are those faces still as masks"
95.note: The essay is titled "George R.R. Martin, The American Homer", subtitled "The Influence of the Oral Tradition". It defines the term the claim uses: "Homer… is well known for the use of epithets, stock phrases that attend a character or concept. Dawn is always rosy-fingered; Athena is grey-eyed", then applies it — "I now think of Martin as one of those minstrels" — and lists Martin's tags: faces "still as masks", "dark with anger", men "corded or thick with muscle", maidens "whose hair shines like spun gold". Fully supported; the word "epithets" is the essay's own.

96.trueWording: stock phrases "give their audience time to absorb"; for a writer, momentum
96.note: Both halves are on the page but from two places. Reader breathing room comes from the NYT block quote the essay adopts: minstrels "fell back on such stock phrases to give their audience time to absorb what had just been sung and to give themselves a moment to think about what they were going to sing next." The writer half is the essayist's own: "for a writer, they come easily off the pen. Very important for maintaining momentum… stock phrases are thermals", and "it's functioning as a literary ummm, as with those minstrels". The minstrel analogy is explicit and central.

97.trueWording: "no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge"
97.note: Page: "Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences. It's shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge of it gets the point across." "low-density sentences" is verbatim and matches the claim's feature label exactly. Cumulative-not-sentence-level is precisely the buckshot figure.

98.trueWording: "almost a shorthand for description… instead of evoking it for us"
98.note: Page: "'Black as night' triggers vision only because it takes longer to read. It's almost a shorthand for description, Martin reminding us to picture the color black instead of evoking it for us. And that's simply because 'black as night' is familiar to us, and we are cognitively lazy with the familiar." Every element of the claim — shorthand, reliance on familiarity, absence of fresh evocation — is present. The embedded fragment "black as night" is verbatim; the surrounding sentence is a paraphrase. Four Martin instances are quoted as evidence.

99.trueWording: "no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest"; other prose "forgettable"
99.note: Page: "all of the top answers referred to passages of dialogue… it's no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest. But the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable." "shine brightest" is verbatim; the claim's "outclassing the narrative passages" is the essay's "the other 60%… is forgettable". Note the essay grounds this in a Reddit thread of readers' favourite passages, not purely its own judgement.

100.trueWording: "The flow is important, it's gotta come out right for him"
100.note: ATTRIBUTION IS OFF — substance holds, the sourcing does not. The flow-over-machining framing is the ESSAYIST's, not Martin's quoted words: "When he describes his writing process, he stresses rhythm"; "The flow is important, it's gotta come out right for him"; and of textualists, "These writers machine their sentences, plane and calibrate them… This is not Martin's way." The actual Martin block quote (January Magazine) says nothing about flow versus sentences — it is about good and bad writing days ("sometimes you eat the bear and sometimes the bear eats you"). So "as quoted by the essay" should be "as characterised by the essay". Counter-evidence worth knowing: the sibling page (imprecision.html) quotes Martin describing exactly the machining the claim denies — "trimming and tightening line by line and word by word… Finish the book, then go through it, cutting, cutting, cutting" — though he frames that as a final polish stage, not drafting.

101.trueWording: "Glowering is a verb for watching, suggesting his beard is covering his face"
101.note: The page never discusses participles or unclear modification — "participle" appears nowhere in the file, and "glowered" in the quoted passage is a finite past-tense verb, not a participle. The essay's actual point is different: given the sentence "He glowered at Arya through his thick beard", since glowering is a verb of watching, "through his thick beard" absurdly implies the beard covers his face; it adds "Echoing of thick is unfortunate." That is a prepositional-phrase and word-repetition complaint. The essay's four named imprecision types are: wrong word (iron for gold), simile physics (melting snow), the thick/glower slip, and redundancy — no loose-participle category. The claim's parenthetical half is real; its load-bearing generalisation is not.

102.trueWording: "Snows melt slowly, over weeks and months. Mist evaporates quickly"
102.note: Exact match of substance. The page quotes the mountain clans "descending from the heights to rob and kill and melting away like snow whenever the knights rode out from the Vale", then comments: "Snows melt slowly, over weeks and months. Mist evaporates quickly, or smoke." The claim's "men vanishing like melting snow though snow melts slowly" is an accurate restatement.

103.trueWording: "I extend this imprecision to his occasional redundancies" — "low, quiet voice"
103.note: Page: "I extend this imprecision to his occasional redundancies. These may happen because he's so focused on the target he's not sure which arrows he's pulling from the quiver", followed by the example "Jon told his uncle in a low, quiet voice." The parenthetical fragment "low, quiet voice" is verbatim. Four further examples of the same shape are listed ("a careful, measuring look"; "low, hushed voices"; "deep and sonorous"; "loved… all the things he loved"). The essay's term is "redundancies", not "doubled modifiers", and it says "occasional" — the claim's "without purpose" is the essayist's diagnosis of unintended repetition, which is fair.

104.trueWording: "I need about 50% less about the cold here"
104.note: LOCATION IS WRONG — fix before use. The quoted line is exact: "I need about 50% less about the cold here." But the two passages it introduces are NOT the prologue: they are Jon at Castle Black ("Chunks of coal burned in iron braziers", "the roughspun blacks that were their everyday wear", "There was scant warmth to be found in Castle Black"), remembering Winterfell. The word "prologue" appears nowhere in the file, and AGOT's prologue is the Will/Waymar Royce ranging beyond the Wall. The cold-hammering observation is genuine; "the prologue" should read "a Jon chapter at Castle Black". Related but separate: the essay makes a second single-sense point immediately after, on anger being alternately cold and "flaring hot".

105.trueWording: Anger is sometimes cold too. Except when it is flaring hot.
105.note: Directly supported. The essay makes this exact point as an imprecision item, then quotes the Castle Black exchange containing 'Jon's anger flared', 'Jon said icily', and 'Jon was cold with rage' — hot and cold vehicles for the same emotion in one passage.

106.trueWording: We know which night this is.
106.note: The essay's only time-marker criticism runs the other direction. Of 'Ned and the girls were eight days gone when Maester Luwin came to her one night', it faults the vague 'one night' as redundant given the elapsed count, and its own proposed rewrite KEEPS the count: 'On her eighth night without Ned and the girls…'. So the page does not hold that elapsed-time markers are stated where context already supplies them; it asks for a more precise marker, not fewer. The essay's separate 'redundancies' section is about doubled adjectives ('low, quiet voice', 'careful, measuring look', 'low, hushed voices') and a repeated bell description — no time markers.

107.trueWording: "Words are wind," is oft-repeated, probably a little bit too much.
107.note: Supported. Whitehead lists it under the book's deeds-not-words theme, and the closing paragraph calls out 'some over-used terms' among the book's dents.

108.trueWording: Martin employs a fairly strict POV structure this time around.
108.note: Partial — read the caveat. The page supports chapters being allotted per POV character and rotating ('Dany, Jon and Tyrion … get a significant number of chapters each but everyone else only gets a few'; 'other POVs only show up when needed'; a 'busy, revolving-door feeling'). But 'fairly strict' on the page means strictness about WHICH characters get chapters, not strictness of narrative technique, and the review never mentions third person or limited narration. The claim borrows the page's exact adjective for a proposition the page does not state.

109.trueWording: with these 'lesser' POVs, there's little to no time for filler
109.note: Supported, and reinforced by the adjacent 'gives some individual storylines and chapters a rather concise, focused feel'. The review adds the converse for the major POVs: Martin occasionally 'dwells on a story point a bit too long'.

110.trueWording: Martin seems to relish some descriptive passages.
110.note: Supported, with the Doom of Valyria named as the example: 'A detailed account of the Doom of Valyria – quite a few books overdue – is spine-crawling and disturbing.' The page says 'detailed', not 'long'; length is the claim's addition.

111.trueWording: Martin breaks off the book on a series of titanic cliffhangers
111.note: Supported and near-verbatim; the page continues 'that dwarf anything seen previously, and only a few story threads find any sense of resolution.' One qualifier the claim drops: Whitehead says the final chapters still make the ending 'impressive, despite the cliffhangers'.

112.trueWording: The rotating-POV structure can lead to frustration
112.note: Supported almost exactly: '…as you are just settling into one character's storyline and are then wrenched halfway across the continent to another character and by the time you get back to the first one it's moved on by several weeks or months.' Listed under the book's flaws.

113.trueWording: sometimes weeks passing between chapters, armies covering hundreds of miles
113.note: The descriptive half is near-verbatim ('armies covering hundreds of miles in the blink of an eye'). The valence is flipped, though: the page files this under flaws — 'The book also feels like it moves a little too quickly at times' — rather than praising rapid forward motion. Whitehead does concede 'On one level this is a good thing', so the claim is not contradicted, only re-coloured.

114.trueWording: individual locations like the Red Keep … come to life quite nicely
114.note: Supported with all three named locations (Red Keep, Winterfell, the Wall). Context worth keeping: this is a concession inside a criticism — the worldbuilding overall 'feels a little sketchy at this point', with the locations coming to life as the exception.

115.trueWording: each point-of-view having a distinct palette and purpose
115.note: Both halves supported in one sentence: 'His ability to convey the interior life of his characters is phenomenal, with each point-of-view having a distinct palette and purpose.' Byline and date on the page match: Matt Maenpaa, July 22, 2011.

116.trueWording: less about the actions … more about response, reaction and decision
116.note: All three parts supported: 'He does not rush'; 'no one has ever accused George R. R. Martin of being concise'; and the response-over-action sentence quoted here. Interiority is carried by 'His ability to convey the interior life of his characters is phenomenal.'

117.trueWording: Martin distracts from the wholesale slaughter … with incredible sensory feasts
117.note: Near-verbatim: 'one of the ways Martin distracts from the wholesale slaughter is with incredible sensory feasts.' The page says 'distracts from'; 'offset' is the claim's addition but is a fair gloss. Byline and date match: Michael R. Underwood, July 27, 2013.

118.trueWording: Like Wagner, he gives each of his characters leitmotifs that recur
118.note: Supported, including the dragons'-eggs image: 'These phrases are like dragons' eggs: the characters keep them close, in the hopes that one day … the words will hatch forth the wisdom they desperately need.' Examples given are 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' and Daenerys' 'If I look back I am lost'. Sourcing caveat: time.com returns HTTP 406 to a direct fetch and the one Wayback capture of this URL is a 403, so text came via WebFetch; I ran a second adversarial pass with an explicit NOT-PRESENT option and both passes agreed on these fragments. Byline confirmed: Lev Grossman, Jul 7, 2011.

119.trueWording: each with its own rhythm, written in its own voice
119.note: Supported, from the count of storylines: '11 major story lines, as well as assorted minor ones, each with its own rhythm, written in its own voice, and each playing off all the others.' The claim drops 'its own rhythm'. Same fetch caveat as 118 — direct fetch 406, text via two agreeing WebFetch passes.

120.trueWording: forgoing the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose
120.note: Grossman (byline Lev Grossman, Jul 7 2011) writes: "If you're watching A Game of Thrones on HBO, you're forgoing the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose." That treats the prose as a distinct pleasure the plot-bearing adaptation cannot supply, which is the claim's substance. Caveat on evidence quality: time.com refused direct fetch (HTTP 406) and the only Wayback capture of this URL is a 403, so the page was read through a summarizing fetch; the sentence was independently corroborated by a Slate review roundup quoting it. No word-for-word check of the whole article was possible.

121.trueWording: men and women slugging it out in the muck
121.note: Full sentence: "It's men and women slugging it out in the muck, for money and power and lust and love," preceded by "A Feast for Crows isn't pretty elves against gnarly orcs." The muck phrase and the grounded/realist register are exact. The Tolkien contrast is real but framed as moral complexity, not register: "Tolkien's work has enormous imaginative force, but you have to go elsewhere for moral complexity." The words "elevated romance" are the claim's gloss, not Grossman's.

122.trueWording: epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama simultaneously
122.note: Source: "Martin has an astonishing ability to focus on epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama simultaneously." Attributed to Martin's ability generally rather than to "the prose" specifically, and the sentence sits beside praise of him as "a tense, surging, insomnia-inflicting plotter and a deft and inexhaustible sketcher of personalities." Substance holds; the word "prose" is the claim's.

123.trueWording: The supernatural plays a role, but only rarely.
123.note: First half is essentially verbatim — the sentence appears exactly as "The supernatural plays a role, but only rarely." The second half is not in this source: Grossman never says the restraint keeps the texture close to historical fiction, and the words "historical fiction" do not appear in the article at all. If the historical-fiction link is needed, cite Fiction Advocate instead, which says Martin "uses fantastic elements sparingly... he initially conceived of the books as historical fiction."

124.trueWording: advice trope of never opening with weather... applies here though
124.note: Both factual halves check out: the post quotes the opening line "The morning had dawned clear and cold, with a crispness that hinted at the end of summer" and calls it "A boring description of the weather?" But the polarity is the opposite of what "defying" implies. Auerbach writes that the advice "stands applies here though, so I've taken the liberty of excising it," then quotes the paragraph without the weather line and says "Much better." He treats it as a flaw Martin got away with, not a rule successfully broken. Do not cite this as endorsement of a weather opening.

125.trueWording: a seven-year old boy going to his first beheading
125.note: The core is directly supported: "We've got a seven-year old boy going to his first beheading," and the quoted passage gives "This was the first time he had been deemed old enough to go with his lord father..." The craft rationale is NOT in the source — Auerbach never discusses point of view, never says the child POV licenses adult explanation, and never connects the narrator's age to exposition. His nearest statement is only "this chapter actually accomplishes a lot. We learn a bit about the world and its history." The "so adult explanation arrives naturally" clause is the claim's own inference.

126.trueWording: amazing how many hints G.R.R.M. dropped in one paragraph
126.note: Both halves supported. Time-stamps: the post quotes "It was the ninth year of summer, and the seventh of Bran's life" and comments "it's apparently the ninth year of summer." Endgame hints in a single paragraph: of the Old Nan paragraph he writes "it's amazing how many hints G.R.R.M. dropped in one paragraph" — Mance Rayder, the wildlings, and "the Others (the White Walkers) and the Long Night, which are incredibly important to the endgame of the entire series."

127.trueWording: pairing the exposition with the dramatic
127.note: Two supporting sentences: "the plot points allow for exposition to happen seamlessly, without losing the reader's interest" and "By pairing the exposition with the dramatic, you reduce the chances of losing the reader." Oliver's framing is "multiple small sources of tension" (Others, Bran's fall, Khal Drogo; and the Nabokov Pnin parallel), which matches the claim's "small dramatic tension."

128.note: Source: "Since Martin has a large cast, he has to use additional tools, such as his emphasis on the importance of names and his extreme (over)use of meaningful nicknames." The parenthetical "(over)use of meaningful nicknames" is verbatim, and the large-cast/exposition framing is explicit in the same sentence.

129.trueWording: obvious foreshadowing with a direwolf who's been killed by a stag
129.note: Both halves near-verbatim. Early and open: "then some obvious foreshadowing with a direwolf who's been killed by a stag" (repeated later as "the aforementioned obvious foreshadowing of the direwolf killed by a stag"). Retroactive recontextualising: "events retroactively reshape characters, they contextualize miniscule asides, and they illuminate the reader's understanding." Note the author's point is that the obviousness "doesn't matter" because the work does not rely on surprise.

130.trueWording: combines some of the best traits of contemporary fantasy
130.note: Martin's own answer, near-verbatim: "One of the things I wanted to do was to write a book that combines some of the best traits of contemporary fantasy with some of the traits of the historical novel." He continues that historical fiction "had an excitement to it and a grittiness and a realness to it that the fantasy novels lacked" and that he wanted "to almost write a historical novel about history that never happened." Only softening: the source says "some of the traits of the historical novel," not "the best traits" of both.

131.trueWording: interviewer: books written from limited third person narrators
131.note: MISATTRIBUTION. The statement is the interviewer's premise, not Martin's words. Verbatim: "NJM: Since the books are written from the perspective of limited third person narrators, we get a lot interactions in the television series that would be impossible in the books. Which one was your favorite?" Martin's answer never mentions point of view, narrators, or the constraint; he only names favourite invented scenes (Robert and Cersei, the Hound and Bronn, Varys and Littlefinger). The claim is true of the article's text but false as "Martin states" / own words.

132.trueWording: not the stuff that advances the plot, but... character parts
132.note: SPLIT — one half is misattributed. "Loves describing food" is the interviewer's premise ("NJM: ...we know from your writing that you love describing food"); Martin's reply is about missing Bayonne pizza and bar pies, and he never says he loves describing food. The second half IS Martin's own words: on cut scenes he says "it's a character scene, and mostly that's what has been cut, not the stuff that advances the plot, but the little character parts," and wishes for more episodes so "we could get in a lot more of these small character scenes." Cite only the character-scene half to Martin.

133.trueWording: I want them to taste the food.
133.note: Supplied quote appears word for word, as the close of "When they sit down at my table, I want them to taste the food." All three sub-claims check out in the quoted foreword: "'gratuitous' usually translates to 'more than I wanted' or 'did not advance the plot'"; "Fiction is about emotion. The heart, not the head." Note the wording is "more than I wanted" (the critic's want), which the claim renders as "more than a given reader wanted" — a fair reading, but not the literal phrase. The article quotes the foreword via Polygon, so this is second-hand from the primary text.

134.trueWording: It's not the destination that matters to me, it's the journey
134.note: Martin's foreword, quoted: "It's not the destination that matters to me, it's the journey," given directly as his answer to why the heraldry, the sex scenes and "the feasts, oh those feasts" are not cut — i.e. the dense description the claim names. One wrinkle: ComicBook's own paraphrase softens it to "the journey is as important as the destination," while Martin's quoted words say the journey matters and the destination does not. The claim tracks Martin, not the paraphrase.

135.trueWording: I want them to live my story, not just read it
135.note: Both halves land. Martin's foreword asks whether it was necessary to mention the knight who 'bore seven golden hedgehogs on a field of dark green' — the claim's 'on dark green' drops 'on a field of', so not verbatim. 'Nothing is gratuitous, as I see it' appears exactly.

136.trueWording: more often than not, they serve a narrative purpose
136.note: First half exact: Walder Frey 'is purposefully serving the King in the North a ho-hum dinner ... as a small act of discourtesy'.
